rationale_evidence.anchor: Names are normative, not descriptive.
rationale_evidence.statement: Ten Chinese-tradition observations against the Kernel's Western assumptions: (1) names are normative not descriptive (Kongzi's zhengming), (2) identity is relational not intrinsic (Xunzi/Confucianism role-based identity), (3) change is continuous not discrete (Daoist hua vs discrete state transitions), (4) contradiction is not necessarily error (Zhuangzi perspectivalism: some contradictions are legitimate differing perspectives), (5) justification is practical (Mohist non-correspondence truth: a claim is true if it works), (6) context is constitutive not external (Zhuangzi/Xunzi), (7) knowing and acting are inseparable (Xunzi: knowledge as capacity not possession), (8) authority is relational/role-based (Confucianism), (9) continuity can be transformation (Zhuangzi: sameness via continuous process, not essence), (10) absence and withdrawal are different (Daoism) -- each posed as a challenge the Kernel's naming/identity/change/contradiction/justification/context/knowledge/authority/continuity/retraction treatment must answer.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Definition defects must be tested.
rationale_evidence.statement: Ten Tarka-Nyaya observations for testing the Kernel boundary: (11) a defining characteristic must avoid avyapti (under-covers), ativyapti (over-covers), asambhava (cannot apply); (12) reason must establish the conclusion via the paksa-sadhya-hetu discipline (proposition/reason/example/application/conclusion); (13) vyapti (invariable concomitance) must be tested in both directions (anvaya/vyatireka); (14) five defective reasons (savyabhicara/viruddha/satpratipaksa/asiddha/badhita) give precise argument-defect vocabulary; (15) absence claims need a counter-correlate (pratiyogi) and a specified kind of absence; (16) viparyaya (erroneous apprehension) shows representation is not truth -- the Kernel must not silently convert representation into semantic truth; (17) samsaya (doubt: mutually contradictory attributes in the same substratum) must be kept distinct from contradiction and error; (18) nigrahasthana (argument failure points) catalogs precise failure modes (abandoning/changing the proposition or reason, etc.); (19) the conclusion (nigamana) must not exceed what the premises establish; (20) abhava (negation/non-existence) has multiple types (absolute/prior/subsequent/locus-specific absence).

rationale_evidence.anchor: Justification is distinct from knowledge.
rationale_evidence.statement: Ten Audi (Western epistemology) observations: (21) justified true belief need not be knowledge (Gettier cases) -- Kernel must handle justified false beliefs differently from knowledge; (22) multiple basic sources of knowledge (perception/memory/introspection/reason/testimony) must not be collapsed; (23) direct (non-inferential) vs indirect (inferential) knowledge must both be handled; (24) justification is prima facie/defeasible (undermining and overriding defeaters); (25) knowledge does not require certainty; (26) internalism vs externalism is a real distinction the Kernel must take a position on; (27) memory preserves but does not create knowledge -- preservation vs generation must be distinguished; (28) testimony transmits knowledge via the attester's knowledge, but testimony-based justification can arise independently; (29) coherence alone is not sufficient for justification; (30) skepticism (hallucination/illusion/dreaming) challenges knowledge claims -- the Kernel must handle uncertainty/fallibility without collapsing into skepticism.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Names prescribe what things should be, not just name what they are.
rationale_evidence.statement: Five most-surprising observations: normative naming (names prescribe, not just classify); contradictions are not necessarily errors (perspectival difference vs logical inconsistency); absence != withdrawal (a claim no longer existing vs no longer assertable); knowing is becoming, not possessing; the smallest boundary may be defined by what it must NOT include (per Tarka's ativyapti/asambhava tests).

rationale_evidence.anchor: The 5 Observations Most Likely to Be Relevant to a Minimal Knowledge Kernel
rationale_evidence.statement: Five observations ranked most relevant to a minimal Knowledge Kernel: identity is relational not intrinsic; justification is practical (consequence-based, not merely internal-consistency-based); change is continuous (versioning/state management must handle continuous transformation, not just discrete states); context is constitutive (must be internal to knowledge representation, not external metadata); naming is normative (must be handled as part of the knowledge itself).

rationale_evidence.anchor: Questions That Conventional DDD Analysis May Not Expose
rationale_evidence.statement: Ten questions conventional DDD analysis may not expose: whether bounded contexts/boundaries are actually stable or shift with context; whether identity is a relation rather than an aggregate property; whether names are normative rather than stable identifiers; whether contradiction can be a legitimate perspective difference rather than an error; whether justification is fundamentally practical/consequence-based rather than internal; whether context is constitutive of knowledge rather than external; whether knowledge is a capacity ('becoming') rather than a possession; whether absence has multiple types rather than being uniform non-existence; whether 'retraction' is a continuous process rather than a deletion event; whether certainty is required for knowledge at all.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The current authority record is strong in provenance but weak in temporal semantics.
rationale_evidence.statement: Measured over 20 observed authority grants: grants with human-act reference 20/20, registeredBy=governance 20/20, grants with immutable commit addressing 13/20, using descriptive artifact references 7/20 — but grants with validity information 0/20, delegation information 0/20, ownership information 0/20. Consequence, in the source's own words: the system 'can establish that authority was registered against a human act, but cannot reliably answer: was this authority valid at a particular historical point in time' — explicitly 'a current-state limitation, not a future-architecture opinion.' By the project's own evidence hierarchy (20260801-1231 §3) this is implementation/persistence-derived evidence (priority 1-3), the strongest evidence class encountered in the corpus so far.

rationale_evidence.anchor: If the grant record has no field in which validity could be expressed, then `0/20` is not twenty observations. It is a single structural fact — the schema cannot represent validity — encountered twenty times.
rationale_evidence.statement: S1-F001's '0/20' validity-information figure reads as a measured empirical rate, inviting 'would a larger sample find some?' — but since the grant record schema has no field capable of expressing validity, 0/20 is one structural fact (schema cannot represent validity) encountered twenty times, not twenty independent observations. Evidence: three independent properties (validity, delegation, ownership) all land at exactly zero across twenty records — the signature of representational absence, not measurement — while properties that ARE representable vary normally (human-act reference 20/20, immutable commit addressing 13/20, descriptive references 7/20); the variation pattern itself distinguishes the two kinds of zero. Connects to the Zero lens: 'absence of the means of expression' is a different thing from 'absence of a value', and S1-F001's original framing conflates them.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The gap is therefore **not a baseline defect that the target model fixes**. It is present in both, which changes its status: from "the current system is behind" to "neither the current system nor the target model time-indexes authority."
rationale_evidence.statement: Reclassifies the finding from NOT ADDRESSED to 'ADDRESSED FOR THE CLAIM, NOT FOR THE AUTHORITY': the temporal-validity gap is not a baseline defect the target model fixes but a property present in both — the question is not whether the model CAN express intervals (it demonstrably can, for claims) but why the concept is applied to one side of an admission (the claim) and not the other (the authority). Explicit governance boundary: 'This finding must not be routed into the active adjudication. The corpus is sealed for that purpose; this is a review record' — research relevance only, no element proposed, Session 1's document not modified.

rationale_evidence.anchor: the two statements are in different grammatical moods, and statements in different moods cannot contradict

A proposal to build X and an observation that existing things lack X are not contradictory; B's residual force is that determinism would be unprecedented in this class of system, a burden on the proposal, not a falsification of it.

rationale_evidence.statement: Three headline findings from applying Nyaya pramana theory, tarka, realism, and debate theory to the Kernel: (1) knowledge is relational/process-based, not a static property -- a claim is knowledge only if generated by the right kind of process (pramana) and defeasible by legitimate doubt; (2) Nyaya's two-tier epistemology (default trust in cognition vs reflective certification when doubt arises) maps onto a 'knowledge core' (trusted default) vs 'adjudication process' (certification) distinction; (3) Nyaya's theory of error is parasitic on truth (error is misplacement of properties onto the wrong object, requiring prior knowledge of the properties/object), directly relevant to the anti-reasoner concept and the representation-!=-truth problem.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Knowledge Requires Four Factors
rationale_evidence.statement: Ten Nyaya observations (Part 1): (1) knowledge requires four unified factors -- knower, known, knowledge source, and knowledge itself (Nyaya-sutra 1.1.1); (2) error is parasitic on truth, a misplacement of a property onto the wrong object (Nyaya-sutra 4.2.35, the shell/silver example); (3) a two-tier epistemology of default trust vs certification when doubt arises (2.1.20); (4) pramanas (perception/inference/analogy/testimony, 1.1.3) are causes of veridical cognition, not conscious justifications -- a causal account of knowledge; (5) inference (linga) has a three-part perception->recollection->inference structure (1.1.5); (6) vyapti (invariable concomitance) must be tested in both anvaya (positive) and vyatireka (negative) directions (1.1.34); (7) absence (abhava) requires a counter-correlative (pratiyogi), you cannot assert non-existence of X without knowing what X would be if it existed (4.2.33); (8) perception is defined by four conditions (sense-object connection, language-independence, inerrancy, definitiveness, 1.1.4); (9) the lamp analogy is interpreted as mutual certification among pramanas, not self-certification (2.1.19), a coherentist element within Nyaya's foundationalism; (10) doubt (samsaya) is the catalyst for inquiry, not a failure state, arising from five distinct triggers (1.1.23).

rationale_evidence.anchor: Knowledge is a Causal Process, Not a Property
rationale_evidence.statement: Five most-surprising observations: knowledge is generated by a causal process, not possessed as a property (a Kernel might need to track the generation process/pramana, not just the claim); error requires prior knowledge of truth (opposite of the Western default-doubt assumption, so error might be modeled as a modified version of truth, not a separate category); default trust, not skepticism, is Nyaya's epistemic starting point (opposite of the Cartesian default-doubt assumption); absence is a real category with structure (counter-correlative plus type: absolute/prior/subsequent/locus-based); doubt has five distinct causal types, not just confidence degrees.

rationale_evidence.anchor: The 5 Observations Most Likely Relevant to a Minimal Knowledge Kernel
rationale_evidence.statement: Five observations ranked most kernel-relevant: the four-factor knower/known/source/knowledge relational structure (a Kernel storing only propositions loses this structure); the two-tier trusted-vs-certified structure; the parasitism thesis (error as modified truth, not a separate category); the counter-correlative requirement for absence/retraction/deletion; the five distinct doubt types (not just a confidence scalar).
